title: How do you build a training matrix for a pharmaceutical site?
description: Build a GMP training matrix for a pharmaceutical site: FDA, EU, TGA and Japan personnel rules, aseptic qualification, effectiveness checks and retention.
shortAnswer: A pharmaceutical site training matrix is built around good manufacturing practice (GMP): every person whose work can affect product quality, including cleaners and maintenance staff, gets basic GMP and duty specific training, with role rows for aseptic operators, visual inspectors and computerized system users. Each cell records its approval, its periodic effectiveness assessment and its retention period, and functions such as laboratories, clinical supply, pharmacovigilance or distribution add rows only where the site performs them.
keyTakeaways: GMP scope is wider than production: EU and PIC/S rules name technical, maintenance and cleaning personnel, and Japan's notice names sterilization and servicing staff.
Every GMP market asks for effectiveness to be assessed or verified, so a completion flag alone does not satisfy the matrix.
Sterile sites need qualification cells, not just training cells: gowning at least annually and aseptic process simulation participation.
Laboratory, clinical, pharmacovigilance and distribution functions bring their own rules. Add them only where the site does that work.
Retention periods differ by rule and market, so store the retention rule with each requirement.

sections.heading: What makes a pharmaceutical training matrix different from other industries?

blocks.text: Three features set it apart: the regulator inspects the training record as evidence of product quality, the rules require training effectiveness to be checked, and named quality leaders must approve the program. A [training matrix](/glossary/training-matrix) on a GMP site is therefore part of the quality system, not an HR register.

In the United States, failure to comply with the drug current good manufacturing practice (CGMP) regulations renders a drug adulterated, and both the drug and the responsible person are subject to regulatory action (21 CFR 210.1) ([eCFR](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-210/section-210.1)). In the European Union, Commission Directive (EU) 2017/1572 requires personnel to 'receive initial and ongoing training, the effectiveness of which shall be verified' (Article 7(4)) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32017L1572)). EU GMP Chapter 2 adds that training programs are approved by the head of Production or the head of Quality Control, as appropriate (paragraph 2.11).

sections.heading: Which GMP rules set the core of the matrix in each market?

blocks.text: Each market has one personnel rule that anchors the matrix, and they converge on the same core: GMP basics, duty specific training, continuing training and records. The differences lie in who approves, who receives reports and how effectiveness is evidenced.

blocks.text: Active pharmaceutical ingredient sites follow ICH Q7 section 3.12 (PIC/S Part II paragraph 3.12), which requires regular training by qualified individuals, records, and periodic assessment ([FDA](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/q7-good-manufacturing-practice-guidance-active-pharmaceutical-ingredients-guidance-industry)).

sections.heading: How should roles be grouped on a GMP site?

blocks.text: Group roles by the areas a person enters and the quality decisions they make, because that is how GMP scopes training. A useful starting set for a finished dose site is the following.

items: **Heads of Production and Quality Control,** who must ensure initial and continuing training of their departments (EU Chapter 2 paragraphs 2.7(vi) and 2.8(vii)) and approve programs.
**Production operators,** split into non sterile and aseptic (grade A and B) where the site makes sterile products.
**Visual inspectors** of filled units, a distinct qualified role on sterile sites.
**QC analysts and microbiologists.**
**Quality assurance staff,** including those who review batch records and run self inspection.
**Engineering, maintenance and cleaning staff,** who enter production and storage areas and are named in scope by EU paragraph 2.10.
**Warehouse staff,** who handle storage and, at some sites, distribution.
**Computerized system users and administrators,** whose access level drives their training under [21 CFR Part 11](/regulations/21-cfr-part-11-training-requirements) section 11.10(i) and EU Annex 11.
**Consultants and contractors,** with records of name, address, qualifications and type of service (211.34; EU paragraph 2.23).
**Visitors and untrained personnel,** who should preferably not enter production and quality control areas and, if unavoidable, are informed in advance and supervised (EU paragraph 2.13).

blocks.text: Japan's 2021 notice on the GMP ordinance confirms the same breadth, naming cleaning, maintenance, sterilization and servicing staff as trainees, and describing training as knowledge plus practical skills ([PMDA](https://www.pmda.go.jp/files/000264441.pdf)).

sections.heading: What does a pharmaceutical site matrix look like?

blocks.text: The matrix below is illustrative, for a hypothetical sterile injectables site that supplies the United States, the EU, Australia and Japan and therefore has to satisfy all four inspectorates. It is cut down to the requirements that most often decide whether a person may work unsupervised.

blocks.text: Under [EU GMP Annex 1](/regulations/eu-gmp-annex-1-sterile-manufacturing-training), unsupervised grade A and B access depends on two cells at once: a passed gowning assessment and successful participation in an aseptic process simulation (Annex 1 paragraph 7.4) ([European Commission](https://health.ec.europa.eu/document/download/e05af55b-38e9-42bf-8495-194bbf0b9262_en?filename=20220825_gmp-an1_en_0.pdf)). Build that as a combined clearance rule so the matrix cannot show an operator as cleared when one half has lapsed. Paragraph 7.6 also requires a disqualification route, with retraining and requalification, which should switch the clearance off automatically.

sections.heading: Which functions add requirements only at some sites?

blocks.text: Laboratories doing regulatory safety studies, clinical trial support, pharmacovigilance, wholesale distribution and biological containment each bring a separate rule set. Add these rows only to the roles that perform the function, and keep them visibly separate from the GMP core so inspectors from different programs can find their own evidence.

items: **Nonclinical laboratory studies.** [Good Laboratory Practice](/regulations/glp-personnel-training-requirements) requires a current summary of training and experience and a job description for each individual (21 CFR 58.29(b)), with a quality assurance unit independent of study personnel.

**Clinical trial activity.** [ICH E6(R3)](/regulations/ich-e6-r3-gcp-training-requirements) requires people involved in a trial to be qualified by education, training and experience, and those using computerized systems to be trained in their use (4.3.2). It sets no fixed refresher interval, so the site must define one.

**Pharmacovigilance.** Under Implementing Regulation (EU) No 520/2012 Article 10, marketing authorization holders keep trained personnel and records, and GVP Module I extends training to adjacent functions such as complaints, medical information, and sales and marketing ([pharmacovigilance training](/regulations/pharmacovigilance-training-requirements)).

**Distribution.** The EU [Good Distribution Practice guidelines](/regulations/good-distribution-practice-training-requirements) require role based GDP training, specific training for temperature sensitive and other special products, and training of staff on insulated box assembly.

**Biological work.** US laboratories handling biological agents follow the BMBL, which expects annual updates and additional training on procedural change, and select agent entities follow 42 CFR 73.15 ([biosafety training](/regulations/biosafety-training-requirements-laboratories)).

sections.heading: How do you prove GMP training was effective rather than just delivered?

blocks.text: Define an effectiveness method for each requirement in the matrix and record its result alongside completion. The EU, PIC/S and Japanese rules all require it, and FDA's 2006 Quality Systems guidance expects training programs to include evaluation of effectiveness and managers to verify that skills are applied ([FDA](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/quality-systems-approach-pharmaceutical-current-good-manufacturing-practice-regulations)).

items: **Observed performance** for SOP driven tasks, rather than signed read and understand records alone; the trade off is set out in [read and understand versus competency based SOP training](/compare/read-and-understand-vs-competency-based-sop-training).
**Qualification results** for aseptic work: gowning plates, APS outcomes and visual inspection qualification are effectiveness evidence in themselves.

**Deviation and CAPA linkage**: where an investigation points to training, the matrix should record the retraining and its check, following [how to use training in a CAPA](/guides/how-to-use-training-in-a-capa).

**Self inspection**: Japan's 2021 notice lists training activities among self inspection items, and PIC/S Part I paragraph 4.29 lists verification of the effectiveness of training among items that need documented procedures.

sections.heading: How long must pharmaceutical training records be kept?

blocks.text: There is no single period: each rule sets its own, so store a retention rule with every requirement. The figures below come from this library's regulation pages.

items: Japan GMP: Article 20(1)(iii) sets five years, or shelf life plus one year if longer, for most records but excepts training records; Article 22 fixes five years for training records at API sites.
US GLP: training summaries and job descriptions follow 21 CFR 58.195, the shortest of 2 years after approval, 5 years after submission, or 2 years after study completion if not submitted.
EU GDP: documents retained for the period in national legislation and at least five years (section 4.2).
EU pharmacovigilance: pharmacovigilance system master file elements kept at least five years after the system is formally terminated (Implementing Regulation 520/2012 Article 12(2)).
US select agents: all Part 73 records, including training, kept for 3 years (42 CFR 73.17(c)).

sections.heading: What is changing for pharmaceutical training in 2026 and 2027?

blocks.text: Most changes affect computerized systems, clinical trials and pharmacovigilance rather than the GMP personnel core. Flag the rows they touch now.

items: **EU Annex 11 revision.** The consultation on revised Chapter 4, Annex 11 and new Annex 22 (artificial intelligence) closed on October 7, 2025. The draft Annex 11 adds system specific training tied to access privileges and recurrent security awareness training; the 2011 Annex 11 remains current as at November 2026.

**ICH E6(R3) Annex 2.** Covering decentralized and pragmatic trial elements, it comes into effect in the EU on January 15, 2027 ([EMA](https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/ich-e6-good-clinical-practice-scientific-guideline)).

**Pharmacovigilance audits.** Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1466 has applied since February 12, 2026 and amends audit and subcontracting rules; Article 10 on training is not among the amended provisions.
**Australia.** The TGA transition period for Annex 1 changes under PE009-17 ran from September 1, 2025 to March 1, 2026, so sterile sites should already hold Annex 1 qualification evidence.
**US biosafety.** A draft NIH Biosafety Policy published on September 14, 2026 would replace the NIH Guidelines once finalized.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each GMP requirement to the SOP, market rule and assessment point behind it, so an SOP revision or a new Annex flags the affected roles and the effectiveness check they need. For the general method see [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix); for converting procedures into assessable training, see [how to convert SOPs into training](/guides/how-to-convert-sops-into-training).

faqs.q: Do cleaning and maintenance contractors need GMP training on a pharmaceutical site?
faqs.a: Yes, where they enter production, storage or quality control areas. EU GMP Chapter 2 paragraph 2.10 names technical, maintenance and cleaning personnel, and Annex 1 extends gowning qualification to cleaning and maintenance staff entering cleanrooms. Record them as roles in the matrix rather than on a separate contractor list.

faqs.q: Is a signed read and understand record enough for SOP training under GMP?
faqs.a: It records completion but not effectiveness, which EU, PIC/S and Japanese rules require to be assessed. Many sites keep read and understand for low risk procedural updates and require observed performance or a knowledge check for tasks with direct quality impact. The matrix should state which method applies to each requirement.

faqs.q: How often must aseptic operators be requalified?
faqs.a: Under EU and PIC/S Annex 1, gowning is reassessed at least annually and each operator should take part in at least one successful aseptic process simulation each year. For manual aseptic operations, each operator needs three consecutive successful simulations initially and revalidation about every six months.

faqs.q: Should GLP, GCP and GMP training be in one matrix?
faqs.a: One role and requirement catalog works well, but tag each requirement with its program so each inspectorate can see its own evidence. Most people on a manufacturing site need only GMP rows; GLP and GCP rows apply only to staff who perform that work.
